title: The Camouflage Hunt: Parent Guide
endLine: Colors that blend into the background are harder to spot.

scenes.tts: Why are so many animals brown or green while others stand out? In this thirty-minute game, your child plays a bird hunting yarn worms. You can see which colors are harder to find when you change the background.
scenes.caption: Why are so many animals brown or green while others stand out? In this thirty-minute game, your child plays a bird hunting yarn worms. You can see which colors are harder to find when you change the background.
scenes.visual: Warm, friendly schematic illustration filling most of the frame: an overhead view of a sunlit green grass patch with softly swaying blades. Two tiny stylized yarn worms—one bright red, one grass-green—rest on the blades; the red pops immediately while the green blends in. A simple schematic bird silhouette glides gently across the top edge. No photos of real children.
scenes.narration: Why are so many animals brown or green while others stand out? In this thirty-minute game, your child plays a bird hunting yarn worms. You can see which colors are harder to find when you change the background.

scenes.visual: The same sunlit grass patch settles into place as four corner shoe icons mark a square. Bold, clean title text 'The Camouflage Hunt' fades in clearly above the patch while grass blades sway slowly.

scenes.tts: What does your child get out of this exercise? They practice making a prediction before testing it. They look closely across a busy patch and sort their finds by color. Then they check what changes on a new background.
scenes.caption: What does your child get out of this exercise? They practice making a prediction before testing it. They look closely across a busy patch and sort their finds by color. Then they check what changes on a new background.
scenes.visual: Same overhead grass patch shifts slightly left to open a clean right-hand side panel. Four simple schematic icons animate in one by one as named: a question mark bubble ('Predict'), a magnifying lens over grass ('Look closely'), four colored tally columns ('Sort and count'), and a grass-to-dirt flip arrow ('Test a change').
scenes.narration: What does your child get out of this exercise? They practice making a prediction before testing it. They look closely across a busy patch and sort their finds by color. Then they check what changes on a new background.

scenes.tts: Cut the yarn yourself into twenty pieces, each about five centimeters long. Make five green, five brown, five red, and five yellow. Mark out a lawn patch about two meters on each side. Use four shoes or short, blunt sticks.
scenes.caption: Cut the yarn yourself into twenty pieces, each about five centimeters long. Make five green, five brown, five red, and five yellow. Mark out a lawn patch about two meters on each side. Use four shoes or short, blunt sticks.
scenes.visual: Schematic workbench overlay on the grass world: friendly illustrated scissors snip four yarn strands into neat rows of five green, five brown, five red, and five yellow short pieces labeled '5 cm'. The four shoes slide out to the corners of the grass patch, with clean arrows showing '2 m x 2 m' and a small cup plus timer icon settling beside the patch.
scenes.narration: Cut the yarn yourself into twenty pieces, each about five centimeters long. Make five green, five brown, five red, and five yellow. Mark out a lawn patch about two meters on each side. Use four shoes or short, blunt sticks.

scenes.tts: Stay with your child and check the patch for hazards first. Choose a spot away from roads. Hunt in shoes and use only soft yarn. Keep it away from children under four. Call nine one one if choking. Keep pets indoors, find all twenty pieces, and wash hands afterward.
scenes.caption: Stay with your child and check the patch for hazards first. Choose a spot away from roads. Hunt in shoes and use only soft yarn. Keep it away from children under four. Call nine one one if choking. Keep pets indoors, find all twenty pieces, and wash hands afterward.
scenes.visual: Show a fenced yard away from the road. An adult checks the grass and points out a different, clear patch. Show shoes and soft yarn. Bring up the text 'Under 4: choking hazard' and then 'Call 911 if choking.' Show pets indoors, all twenty pieces back in the tray, and hands being washed.
scenes.narration: Stay with your child and check the patch for hazards first. Choose a spot away from roads. Hunt in shoes and use only soft yarn. Keep it away from children under four. Call nine one one if choking. Keep pets indoors, find all twenty pieces, and wash hands afterward.

scenes.tts: Show your child one worm of each color. Ask, "If you were a bird, which color would you find first?" Write down their guess. While they turn away, scatter all twenty worms on top of the grass.
scenes.caption: Show your child one worm of each color. Ask, "If you were a bird, which color would you find first?" Write down their guess. While they turn away, scatter all twenty worms on top of the grass.
scenes.visual: Line up one yarn worm of each color on the tray. Show the parent writing down the guess. With the child represented by a simple schematic bird facing away, place all twenty pieces on top of the grass.
scenes.narration: Show your child one worm of each color. Ask, "If you were a bird, which color would you find first?" Write down their guess. While they turn away, scatter all twenty worms on top of the grass.

scenes.tts: Say go. Give your child thirty seconds to put worms in the cup, one at a time. Red and yellow usually go first. Green and brown are often left. Record the count for each color and recover every piece. Play three rounds, then total the counts by color.
scenes.caption: Say go. Give your child thirty seconds to put worms in the cup, one at a time. Red and yellow usually go first. Green and brown are often left. Record the count for each color and recover every piece. Play three rounds, then total the counts by color.
scenes.visual: Show a thirty-second timer and one worm at a time going into the cup. Label the tally sheet 'Example' and show one possible round with red and yellow found more often. Return every piece to the tray. Fill the next round columns in turn and highlight the total for each color.
scenes.narration: Say go. Give your child thirty seconds to put worms in the cup, one at a time. Red and yellow usually go first. Green and brown are often left. Record the count for each color and recover every piece. Play three rounds, then total the counts by color.

scenes.tts: For the next hunt, choose bare dirt or a patterned rug. Before you scatter the worms, ask your child, "Which color do you think will hide best here?" Write down their guess. Take a moment to make your own prediction.
scenes.caption: For the next hunt, choose bare dirt or a patterned rug. Before you scatter the worms, ask your child, "Which color do you think will hide best here?" Write down their guess. Take a moment to make your own prediction.
scenes.visual: Change the view from grass to bare dirt, with a small inset of a patterned rug as another option. Keep all twenty yarn worms in the tray beside the patch. Show the parent noting the guess and bring up the question 'Which color hides best here?'
scenes.narration: For the next hunt, choose bare dirt or a patterned rug. Before you scatter the worms, ask your child, "Which color do you think will hide best here?" Write down their guess. Take a moment to make your own prediction.

scenes.visual: Hold the question 'Which color hides best here?' over the empty dirt patch for four and a half seconds. Keep the yarn worms in the tray and let a little dust drift silently across the patch.

scenes.tts: Scatter the same worms and run another thirty-second hunt. Count by color and find every leftover worm. Check your guesses. Which colors were found least often on each background? Brown often hides well on brown dirt. When a color blends into the background, it can be harder to spot.
scenes.caption: Scatter the same worms and run another thirty-second hunt. Count by color and find every leftover worm. Check your guesses. Which colors were found least often on each background? Brown often hides well on brown dirt. When a color blends into the background, it can be harder to spot.
scenes.visual: Move the worms from the tray to the dirt and start the timer. Show one possible hunt with brown found least often. Label both sets of tallies 'Example.' Highlight the lowest count within each background, including all colors tied for lowest. Gather every piece back into the tray.
scenes.narration: Scatter the same worms and run another thirty-second hunt. Count by color and find every leftover worm. Check your guesses. Which colors were found least often on each background? Brown often hides well on brown dirt. When a color blends into the background, it can be harder to spot.

scenes.tts: Close by asking, "Which worms would still be alive at the end of the day?" Real animals can pass their colors to their young. If animals with a matching color survive more often and have more young, that color can become more common.
scenes.caption: Close by asking, "Which worms would still be alive at the end of the day?" Real animals can pass their colors to their young. If animals with a matching color survive more often and have more young, that color can become more common.
scenes.visual: Show the two example patches from the hunts. On the grass side, show the surviving worms and their same-colored young in a simple schematic labeled 'If survivors have more young.' Show how the share of matching worms can grow across generations while the color of each individual worm stays the same.
scenes.narration: Close by asking, "Which worms would still be alive at the end of the day?" Real animals can pass their colors to their young. If animals with a matching color survive more often and have more young, that color can become more common.
